narrative:
The model predicted an 88.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction heavily toward failure. While the average accepted student ranked around the middle of their class (decile near 6), you placed in the bottom decile. This low ranking signaled to the model a much higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. At 25, your score sits well below the average of 37 among accepted students, indicating the model saw this as a significant obstacle to passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.5 it is stronger than the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this helped reduce the predicted risk somewhat. However, its positive effect was not large enough to overcome the combined impact of your class ranking and LSAT score.

Given these results, you should focus on improving your bar exam readiness before reapplying. Consider retaking the LSAT for a higher score, or enrolling in a strong bar-preparation course that targets the specific skills where your academic record shows weakness. Strengthening those areas will give you the best chance of a successful future application. (248 words)
